title: Indian Startup Miraqules Wins SLINGSHOT 2026 Grand Prize in Singapore
excerpt: The Indian medtech's StopBleed powder, designed to stop severe bleeding within about a minute, beat more than 5,000 startups to take the S$400,000 Startup SG Grant at SWITCH, according to CNA.
body:
• Miraqules MedSolutions, an Indian medtech startup, has been named Grand Winner of SLINGSHOT 2026, Enterprise Singapore's global deep-tech pitching competition, at the Grand Finals held during SWITCH in Singapore.
  • CNA reported Miraqules beat more than 5,000 startups from around the world; the Grand Winner receives a S$400,000 Startup SG Grant, according to the competition's official prize structure.
  • Its StopBleed powder, made from nanofibrous biomaterials, is designed to stop severe bleeding within about a minute, according to the company.
  • The product is not yet commercially approved; clinical validation and regulatory clearance are still ahead.

SINGAPORE — An Indian medtech startup whose powder is designed to halt severe bleeding within about a minute has won the top prize at SLINGSHOT 2026, the global deep-tech pitching competition run by Enterprise Singapore during the Singapore Week of Innovation and Technology (SWITCH).

Miraqules MedSolutions emerged as the Grand Winner at the Grand Finals on October 29, beating more than 5,000 startups from around the world, according to CNA, which interviewed founder and chief executive Sabir Hossain after the win. The Grand Winner receives a S$400,000 Startup SG Grant, according to the competition's official prize structure; the Top 10 domain winners, revealed on October 28, each receive S$80,000. Miraqules competed in the Health and Biomedical domain. SLINGSHOT's 2026 edition offered more than S$2.2 million in grant prizes in total.

A powder built to buy minutes

Miraqules' product, StopBleed, is a powder based on nanofibrous biomaterials made from clinically accepted biopolymers. The company says its biomaterials can stop bleeding within a minute of application, and it is developing them for injuries of any severity, size and shape. The company positions the technology for the settings where uncontrolled bleeding kills fastest: road accidents, battlefields, disaster zones and rural areas far from a trauma centre.

The company has lab and office space at the KIIT Technology Business Incubator in India and a long record in India's publicly backed startup ecosystem, including a Biotechnology Ignition Grant from the Department of Biotechnology's BIRAC and a place among the top startups at Global Bio-India, according to its own site.

Why Singapore, and what comes next

SLINGSHOT is Enterprise Singapore's flagship competition for deep-tech startups, run through the SWITCH festival, and it is designed to plug winning companies into Singapore's research, hospital and investor networks. For an Indian medtech at Miraqules' stage, that matters as much as the grant: the company still has to complete clinical validation and win regulatory approvals before StopBleed can be sold, and Singapore offers a route to hospital pilots and Southeast Asian markets.

The win also continues a pattern Indian founders know well. India's medtech sector has produced globally competitive devices before, but trauma care — where most preventable deaths occur before a patient reaches surgery — has drawn less venture money than diagnostics or hospital software. A hemostat designed to work within a minute is aimed squarely at that gap, and at the ambulances, first responders and military medics who reach patients first.

The honest caveat

StopBleed's headline claims rest on the company's own pre-clinical work, not on published human trials, and no regulator has yet cleared the product for sale. Plenty of promising wound-care technologies have stalled between early studies and approval. What SLINGSHOT's judges have certified is the strength of the science and the size of the problem — Miraqules describes its technology and history on its company site. The clinical proof is the test still to come.

For the Indian diaspora's large community of clinician-founders and health-tech investors in Singapore and the United States, the result is a marker: an Indian deep-tech medical device has beaten a global field of more than 5,000 startups on a Singapore stage. Whether it reaches ambulances will be decided by trials, not pitch decks.
